scores.rationale: Good points: the scope cut is right (no localization, no EFE, the gradient trick demoted with a citation). It states plainly that mIoU equals averaging. It admits that its F2 estimator is almost NormLift's reliability. Gates have dated fallbacks, including a switch to Bonn by Oct 14. Its 'hidden' class of occluded Gaussians in the stale ground truth is careful. It has the lightest load: about 25.5 pd over 7 weeks. Problems: (1) The optimised deterministic field (the Feature-3DGS-style row) is only a stretch goal. Tab I then compares only against averaging, CSS and 2D. A reviewer will ask whether a trained field gets higher mIoU. (2) The RIO10 test is cut to N=4 scenes, and its success test is '>= 3 of 4', which is weak evidence. (3) There is no depth-residual baseline and no threshold-sensitivity plot, while the math report says the thresholds are hand-set. (4) Its F2 with m0=0 is exactly NormLift's reliability. I measured max difference 0.0 and Spearman 1.0 (see recommendation). So C2's novelty rests only on counting views and on the epistemic channel. The plan admits this but does not add a gate for it. Feasibility risks: G2 needs 8 Replica fits in W3 (Oct 12-18) while USGLoc still holds the GPU (13604/16303 MiB used at 22:51 today). RIO10 access time is unknown. The Replica download is feasible: the Semantic-NeRF zip is 6.76 GB, about 9.4 h at 200 KB/s (my HEAD check).

Strongest evidence design. Tab I has every fair row: 2D MaskCLIP, an optimised deterministic field, weighted mean + NormLift, and CSS with variance and MI/entropy. The change table has photometric residual, depth residual, scalar variance, CSS, NormLift and raw r̄, and keeps rows where a baseline wins. RIO10 test uses all 7 scenes. Ablations remove one part at a time and rename the method to what is left. There is a sensitivity plot and a gate that re-runs one scene from saved commands (G5). The rule 'never submit with val-only results' is right. Gate G1 on Oct 9 is a cheap CPU check on real CLIP before any GPU work: this is the best risk control of the three plans. Weaknesses: (1) F2's joint prior with m0=0 and c0=beta is exactly NormLift's reliability (max difference 0.0 in my check). The plan does not say so, and its own NormLift row will likely show no AUSE_ale gain. (2) It adds many parts (joint prior, within/across split, change score, depth re-admission check), which makes the method complex; T4 ablations partly offset this. Feasibility is the problem. The plan needs about 39 pd (31 code + 8 writing) out of an assumed 45 pd for one student. That leaves 3 days of buffer before the Nov 30 IROS-transfer limit, on a GPU USGLoc holds until mid-October. The Jan 29 backup keeps the RA-L submission but loses the IROS 2027 transfer.

Good points: F2 uses the math report's view-level Kish ρ̂ estimator. It is a little more distinct from NormLift (Spearman 0.978 on random inputs, vs 1.0 for the joint prior). It has a clear boundary with USGLoc, a gate-wrapper script, and a rule not to submit if G2 fails too. The 7-Scenes false-alarm row (E4) is a useful idea: a static-scene control for the change detector. Weaknesses: (1) NormLift is only cited, never measured, in either table, yet it is the closest overlap for C2. E3 also lacks depth-residual and NormLift rows. (2) E4 reuses USGLoc's maps on USGLoc's headline dataset. That increases the overlap a shared reviewer will see. The venue report says 'fitting UAGS's own maps is better'. E4 also assumes 7-Scenes has no scene change ('every flag is false'), which no report checked. (3) It imports usgloc through PYTHONPATH and copies usgloc/metrics.py, so the UAGS code depends on a sibling repo that is still changing. It also needs care in an anonymous submission. (4) D1 recommends keeping a localization row (E8), which the venue report advises against. (5) 'mIoU equals the averaged field by construction' stops being exact once F1 reweights by view. Feasibility: about 29.5 pd in 7 weeks. It needs 18 fits in W3 and E4 GPU jobs in W2, while USGLoc still uses about 13.6 GB. RIO10 must be on disk by Oct 11, and the access time is unknown (the URL is redacted in ACE-G's setup_rio10.py:6,31; RIO10 README:9 requires a Google Form).

best_elements.element: Gate G1 (Oct 9): a CPU replay on real MaskCLIP features before any GPU job. Pass needs a change AUROC above 0.591/0.633 and an evidence count n that does not depend on resolution. On failure, rename u_ale to 'ambiguity' and consolidate only on the change score.
best_elements.why: The main risk in all three plans is that real CLIP features do not separate change (math E9: AUROC 0.59-0.73). This gate tests that risk in week 2 for almost no cost, with no GPU and no new data.

best_elements.element: The full fair-baseline set with shared geometry and features. T1: optimised deterministic field, NormLift, CSS with variance and MI/entropy. T3: photometric and depth residual, scalar variance, raw r̄. Ablations remove one part at a time, then the method is renamed to what remains. Plus a sensitivity plot and gate G5 (re-run one scene from the saved commands).
best_elements.why: This answers the reviewer questions the reports predict: 'your mIoU equals averaging', 'NormLift already does this', 'CSS already splits the two', and 'the thresholds are hand-set'. It also keeps rows where a baseline wins.

best_elements.element: The 'honest core fact' framing (same mIoU, better uncertainty), plus an explicit note that F2 with m0=0 is almost NormLift's reliability. Fallback titles are tied to the gates, and the switch to Bonn has a fixed date (Oct 14).
best_elements.why: It avoids claims the reports do not support (code mismatch 6, sota C1/C2). It also gives the student a clear decision at each gate.

best_elements.element: A third, 'hidden' class for stale ground truth: Gaussians that stay behind the seq02 depth in every update view are left out of AP and reported separately.
best_elements.why: Without it, stale-content AP counts occluded but unchanged Gaussians as errors. The math report (E9) names occlusion as one of the five causes of low r̄.

best_elements.element: F2 as the view-level Kish estimator ρ̂² = (n_K r̄² − 1)/(n_K − 1), undefined when n_K ≤ 1, with a unit test on uniform directions (math C2-c: 0.062 / 0.021).
best_elements.why: This is the math report's recommended fix for E7. It ranks Gaussians a little differently from NormLift (Spearman 0.978, vs exactly 1.0 for the joint prior with m0=0), which leaves some room for a distinct contribution.

best_elements.element: A static-scene false-alarm control for the change detector (E4), and 'if G2 also fails, do not submit on Nov 15'.
best_elements.why: Measuring false positives where nothing changed is the natural control for a change detector. The stop rule protects against submitting weak evidence.

fatal_flaws.flaw: F2 (joint conjugate prior, A_d(κ̂) = ‖R+m0‖/(n+c0)) is exactly NormLift's reliability r̄·N/(N+β) when m0=0 and c0=β. I checked: max difference 0.0, Spearman 1.0 (estim_equiv.log). The plan does not say this. Its own T1/T3 NormLift row will then show no AUSE_ale gain unless the counting in F1 or the text prior m0 makes a difference. This must be flagged and tested as a gate, or the aleatoric-channel claim falls apart in review.

Schedule: about 39 pd of work in an assumed 45 pd for one student, with 3 days before the Nov 30 limit. GPU contention (13604/16303 MiB used at 22:51 today) and RIO10 access delays are not counted in those pd. The realistic outcome is the Jan 29 backup, which loses the IROS 2027 transfer.

The optimised deterministic field is only a stretch goal, and the RIO10 test has N=4 scenes (success = '>= 3 of 4'). The tables would lack the strongest fair baseline and have little statistical weight. A reviewer can ask for both. Its F2 has the same NormLift equivalence as B's, but here it is disclosed.

NormLift, the closest concurrent overlap for C2, is cited but never measured. E4 reuses USGLoc's 7-Scenes maps and imports its code, which increases the cross-paper overlap the venue report warns about. E4 also assumes 7-Scenes has no scene change, which no report checked. D1 keeps a localization row against the venue report's advice.

Three gaps no plan addresses. (1) F3 centres image features before normalising, but no plan says how text queries are scored afterwards. Centering shifts each class score by m·t_c, so the argmax and mIoU can change (not checked). Keep a raw accumulator for queries and centre only for dispersion and change, or centre the text side too and test it on val. (2) F1's weight w_v = min(1, m_v/m0) uses pixel mass m_v, which grows about 16× from ds4 to full resolution. The resolution-invariance unit tests (A <1%, B <5%, C 'same') will fail unless m0 is set as a fraction of image area. (3) 'mIoU equal to averaging by construction' stops being exact once F1 reweights by view. The averaged baseline must use the same view weights, or the claim must be softened.

recommendation:
Recommendation: build a hybrid. Use B's evidence design, A's scope and dates, and C's estimator. Target submission Sun 2026-11-15, hard stop Mon 2026-11-30 (weekdays checked with `date -d`, dates.txt).

1. **Scope.** Take it from A/B: no localization table, no 7-Scenes localization, no EFE, gradient trick cited as Joseph et al. Drop C's E8 localization row. Keep C's E4 static false-alarm control only if it uses UAGS's own fitted geometry, not usgloc/maps, and only if 7-Scenes is first shown to have no scene change. Otherwise use static Replica Seq_2 as the false-alarm control.
2. **Estimator.** Put C's view-level Kish ρ̂ and A/B's joint prior side by side on val. Add a gate: the chosen u_ale must beat the NormLift row on AUSE_ale on val. If neither does, say in the paper that the aleatoric channel equals NormLift's reliability with views counted, and move the claim to the view-level epistemic channel and the change test. With m0=0 and c0=1, the joint prior equals NormLift's reliability exactly: `python3 estim_equiv.py` gives max difference 0.0 and Spearman 1.0. Kish vs NormLift gives Spearman 0.978 (estim_equiv.log).
3. **Baselines and gates.** Take B's baseline set: the optimised deterministic field is required, not a stretch goal. NormLift and depth residual go in both tables. Keep B's G1 CPU gate on Oct 9, the one-part-at-a-time ablations, the sensitivity plot, G5 reproducibility, and 'never submit val-only'. From A, keep the hidden-class stale ground truth.
4. **Test size.** Run RIO10 test on all 7 scenes if disk allows. Otherwise use N=4 and say so.
5. **Fix the shared gaps before coding F1/F3.**
   - Set m0 as a fraction of image area.
   - Decide how text queries are scored after centering.
   - Make the averaged baseline use the same view weights.
6. **Today.**
   - Submit the RIO10 Google Form. The URL is redacted in ACE-G's setup_rio10.py (lines 6 and 31), and RIO10 README line 9 requires the form.
   - Start the Replica download. `curl -sIL 'https://www.dropbox.com/sh/9yu1elddll00sdl/AAC-rSJdLX0C6HhKXGKMOIija?dl=1'` gives content-length 6,762,780,327 bytes for the whole Semantic-NeRF folder zip (replica_head.txt). That is about 9.4 h at 200 KB/s.
   - Start no GPU work: `nvidia-smi` showed 13604/16303 MiB used at 22:51 on 2026-09-28, and `df -h` showed 48G free (gpu_disk.txt).
   - Compile on Overleaf: `ls ~/.local/bin/tectonic` fails.
7. **What to expect.** Even the best version has thin novelty. The gradient trick is scooped, μ* equals training-free lifting, and u_ale is close to NormLift. Acceptance therefore depends on two results: the RIO10 change result beating the photometric and depth residuals, and the cross-AUSE disentanglement. If either fails on val, use A's fallback title and consider a later RA-L window rather than submitting weak evidence.

scores.rationale:
Workload is 18.5 code pd + 7 writing pd = 25.5 pd, against 34 workdays from Sep 29 to Nov 15 (python workday count). That fits, but only if the student works mostly on UAGS. Evidence says they are still busy with USGLoc. The same author (thanhnguyencanh <<email redacted>>) wrote the UAGS commits and the USGLoc commits, and USGLoc got a new commit today (adea106, 2026-09-28 22:03). USGLoc also has 15 uncommitted files (`git -C usgloc log -5`; `git status --short | wc -l` = 15). So real capacity before about mid-October is lower than the plan assumes.

What the plan gets right:
- Its claims match the reports. F1-F10 map to math E5, E7-E12, E15 and E16, and to code risks 1-3.
- It says outright that μ* is the plain weighted mean, so it claims equal mIoU.
- It admits that with m0=0 the joint-prior estimator is NormLift's reliability. From math E10, A_d(κ̂) = ‖R‖/(n+c0) has the same form as NormLift's r̄·N/(N+β). Because AUSE is rank-based, u_ale would tie NormLift's AUSE whenever n is counted the same way. So F1 (counting evidence in views) is the only real difference, and the paper must say so.
- It uses the decode-first query, so no evaluation vocabulary leaks into the PCA basis.
- Its 4 RIO10 test scenes (02, 03, 05, 07) have 14,035 val frames, against 29,486 for B and C (awk over rio10_stats.txt). That lowers the disk risk.

Hidden dependencies:
- Each RIO10 seqXX.zip bundles the train, val and all hidden test sequences. The README (data scratch rio10_readme.md l.13-63) says so, and the models zip also has a mesh per sequence. Scenes 03 and 07 are the second- and third-largest val sequences (5,143 and 5,473 frames).
- It is not checked whether the meshes of different sequences are aligned to one frame. The README only says the poses are aligned.

Weaknesses:
- The optimised-field baseline is only a stretch goal.
- Tab II has no depth-residual baseline.
- N=4 test scenes.
- The '23 GPU-h' figure is an assumption. The GPU is also overestimated for fits: the USGLoc plan (l.151) says '~2 min/scene maps', and the usgloc/maps mtimes are 2 min apart. Memory co-residency is the real limit (nvidia-smi 22:49: 13,604/16,303 MiB at 92%).

The Replica risk is now small. The Semantic-NeRF Dropbox zip is 6,762,780,327 bytes (HEAD, judge/dbx_head.txt) and downloaded at 10.3 MB/s (judge/dbx_range.txt), so about 11 min.

This plan is the strongest on evidence: an early CPU math gate G1 on Oct 9, residual baselines (photometric and depth), NormLift and CSS with MI/entropy, a remove-one-part ablation loop, a sensitivity sweep, 7 RIO10 test scenes, an optimised-field row and a one-scene rerun check at G5. That gives the best chance of acceptance if it is finished.

The time budget does not hold:
- Work is 25.5-31 code pd + 8 writing pd = 33.5-39 pd, against 44 workdays to Nov 27 (python count).
- It rests on the plan's own assumption of '5 pd per week'. The git logs show the same student still committing to USGLoc today, with 15 files uncommitted.
- Only 3 days remain before the Nov 30 IROS-transfer limit (Nov 27 + 5 months = Apr 27, 2027). Any slip moves the paper to Jan 29, which is still a valid RA-L route, but without IROS.

Hidden dependencies:
- T3 'mIoU on unchanged regions' needs a class map for RIO10's instances.txt / labels.ply. The data report marks this 'not checked', and it may need the separate 3RScan form.
- The 7 test scenes include the 4 largest val sequences (seq09 7,245 frames, seq10 7,307, seq07 5,473, seq03 5,143). Each seqXX.zip also carries every hidden test sequence. RIO10 sizes are not checked, and 48 GB is free (`df -h /home`).
- G1 is a replay of simulated change (math C3b), not a real rearrangement, so it is a weak early gate.
- The same estimator equals NormLift, as in plan A. That is fine only because NormLift is a measured row here.

Claims not backed by the reports: the 2 cm stale threshold and the 5% resolution-invariance bound. The plan labels both as assumptions.

Workload is 21.5 code pd + 8 writing pd = 29.5 pd, against 34 workdays to Nov 15. That is tighter than plan A, and it rests on the same shared-student problem (same git author on USGLoc, commit today).

Weeks 3-5 are front-loaded: 8 Replica and 10 RIO10 fits in Oct 12-18, with G1 needing RIO10 data by Oct 11. The RIO10 form turnaround is not checked. USGLoc heavy GPU use is expected until at least mid-October (venue D estimate).

Reuse problems:
- Task 6 imports the live usgloc/mapping.py through PYTHONPATH. usgloc changes daily (adea106 today, 15 uncommitted files), so UAGS results would depend on another paper's uncommitted code. That breaks rule I1 (results reproduce from saved commands) and can break at any time.
- E4 puts 7-Scenes back into UAGS on USGLoc's own maps. Venue C rated silent map reuse as a High overlap. Disclosed, it is allowed, but it adds nothing a static Replica control could not give.
- E4's ground truth 'every flag is false' is an assumption. Nobody checked whether 7-Scenes train and test sequences are free of scene change.

The plan also leaves NormLift out as a measured baseline in E1 and E3, even though it is the closest concurrent work (sota §2, C2 overlap). A reviewer will ask for it.

F5 uses joint image+text PCA only. It does not say which text set is used. If that set is the evaluation vocabulary, the 'open-vocabulary' claim is weakened.

D1(b) keeps a localization ablation row. Venue C allows this, but it adds overlap with USGLoc.

Good parts:
- The gate wrapper is task 1.
- The AUSE definition is shared with USGLoc, which fixes the two-definitions issue in code mismatch 10.
- The view-level Kish ρ̂ is 'undefined' at n_K ≤ 1, which correctly means 'no information'.

best_elements.element: A 'hidden' class for Gaussians behind the seq02 surface in every update view, left out of stale AP and reported separately
best_elements.why: Occlusion is one of the five causes of dispersion in math E9. Without this class, occluded but unchanged Gaussians count as errors or as stale content and bias AP either way. Neither B nor C handles it.

best_elements.element: State the equivalences openly: μ* equals the weighted mean (same mIoU), and the joint-prior estimator with m0=0 equals NormLift's reliability. Then compete only on uncertainty quality and view-level evidence.
best_elements.why: Code mismatch 6 and sota §2 make both facts easy for a reviewer to find. Saying them first removes the most likely reject reason, and it points the experiments at the one real difference (F1, view counting).

best_elements.element: Decode-first text query μ*ᵀ(Bᵀt), without renormalising Bᵀt
best_elements.why: It fixes the 11% text-energy problem (math E15) without fitting PCA on the evaluation vocabulary. That keeps the open-vocabulary claim clean. C's joint-PCA-only fix risks leaking the vocabulary.

best_elements.element: Early CPU-only math gate G1 on Oct 9, before any data download or GPU job, with the fallback wording 'rename u_ale to ambiguity' ready
best_elements.why: It tests the riskiest assumption (a change signal on real CLIP features, AUROC 0.59-0.75 today) at almost no cost, while the GPU is taken by USGLoc.

best_elements.element: Depth-residual and photometric-residual baselines in the change table, plus 'keep any row where a baseline wins'
best_elements.why: On RIO10 the map geometry is fixed, and moved objects cause large geometric and photometric residuals. These are the baselines a reviewer will demand. Beating only scalar variance would not convince anyone.

best_elements.why: It keeps the claims honest after 10 fixes (F1-F10), and it matches the reproducibility check reviewers increasingly ask for.

best_elements.why: USGLoc's own gates give up and launch anyway after 5.3 h (venue D), so a UAGS job holding memory can crash USGLoc. A shared, scripted gate protects both papers.
